Interaction name: accordion-walkthrough

Purpose. Give the learner a sequence of steps they can work through one at a time, reading the detail and a short activity for each without the others competing for attention.

Content — complete each slot with your material. The interaction's built-in labels and prompts stay as they are.

Title: …

Body copy (intro): …

Step 1 title: …

Step 1 short description (shown next to the title): …

Step 1 body paragraph: …

Step 1 "Try it" activity prompt: …

Step 2 title: …

Step 2 short description (shown next to the title): …

Step 2 body paragraph: …

Step 2 "Try it" activity prompt: …

(repeat the block for each step)

You can place 2–8 steps using this interaction.

When the content is complete: copy and paste the whole brief into the SB and assign a CU ticket.

Technical details for the LT — don't update unless you want the interaction to behave differently.

Layout. The title with the body copy beneath. Below, a single bordered accordion of numbered rows. Each row header carries a numbered circle badge, the bold step title with its short dash-separated description, and a chevron at the right. The open row's body holds the body paragraph and a "Try it" callout strip (icon, "Try it" label, the activity prompt).

Interaction. Clicking a closed row header opens it and closes whichever row was open; clicking the open row's header closes it. The chevron flips when a row opens, and the open header inverts to the dominant brand colour. Keyboard: headers are native buttons, Enter or Space toggles, arrow up/down (plus Home/End) move focus between the headers. Each toggle re-reports the document height.

States. At most one row open at a time, zero open is allowed. Row one is open by default. All bodies exist in the markup; closed bodies are hidden. Open state is carried by aria-expanded, the flipped chevron, and the inverted header.

Layout. The title with the body copy beneath. Below, a segmented toggle with two options: "1 Before — poor example" and "2 After — improved example". Below the toggle, one panel. The before panel holds a text tag "POOR EXAMPLE", the poor-example mock built from placeholder boxes, and the list of issue notes, each with a cross icon. The after panel holds a text tag "IMPROVED", the improved mock, and the list of fix notes, each with a tick icon.

Build a three-line placeholder query across four selection-based rounds: pick a code fragment, see it land in a dark console, review a three-row result table, then advance to a completion strip.

The brief template

This is the brief template for the interaction above. Copy it, fill in the Content slots with your material, and leave the technical details unless you want the interaction to behave differently.

Interaction name: code-lab

Purpose. Give the learner a way to build a short query step by step by choosing code fragments — seeing each choice land in a console and return a result — without any free typing.

Content — complete each slot with your material. The interaction's built-in labels and prompts stay as they are.

Title: …

Body copy (intro): …

Console query template (the code lines, with one slot per round): …

Round 1 task (one line): …

Round 1 fragment options (one per line, 3 chips): …

Round 1 correct fragment: …

Round 1 result table (3 rows or fewer): …

Round 1 explanation (one line): …

Round 2 task (one line): …

Round 2 fragment options (one per line, 3 chips): …

Round 2 correct fragment: …

Round 2 result table (3 rows or fewer): …

Round 2 explanation (one line): …

(repeat the block for each round)

Completion line (shown when the lab is finished): …

You can place 2–6 rounds using this interaction.

When the content is complete: copy and paste the whole brief into the SB and assign a CU ticket.

Technical details for the LT — don't update unless you want the interaction to behave differently.

Layout. The title with the body copy beneath. A row of progress chips ("Round 1"–"Round N") with a "Round x of N" line beneath. Below that, a dark console-styled panel (the page itself stays light) showing the query template, whose fragment slots start as dotted placeholders. Below the console, one round panel at a time: the round heading, its one-line task, the clickable code-fragment chips, and a result area — the result table, the one-line explanation, and a "Next round" button (the last round's reads "Finish lab") — hidden until a fragment is chosen. After the last round, a completion strip with a tick icon, the completion line, and a "Restart lab" button.

Interaction. Clicking a fragment chip inserts that fragment into its console slot instantly (no typewriter effect) — the filled slot gets a solid plate and bold weight, the chosen chip gets a pressed state with a tick icon (never colour alone) — and reveals that round's result table, explanation, and next button. The learner can change their choice before advancing; the console updates. "Next round" hides the current round, shows the next, marks the finished chip done with a tick, and updates the progress line. "Finish lab" shows the completion strip and marks all chips done. "Restart lab" resets the console slots, chips, and rounds to the start. All controls are native buttons, fully keyboard operable; focus moves to the revealed next button and then to each new round's first chip.

States. Rounds are shown one at a time, round 1 the default, plus a final completed state. Per round, the result area is hidden or revealed, and exactly zero or one of its chips is pressed. Each console slot is unfilled (dotted placeholder) or filled. Progress chips are upcoming, current (thick border and bold), or done (filled with tick).

The brief template

Interaction name: drag-drop-classifier

Purpose. Give the learner a way to practise classifying items by sorting scenario cards into labelled category zones and getting per-card feedback on where each one belongs.

Content — complete each slot with your material. The interaction's built-in labels and prompts stay as they are.

Title: …

Body copy (intro): …

Zone 1 name: …

Zone 1 one-line definition: …

Zone 2 name: …

Zone 2 one-line definition: …

(repeat for each zone)

Card 1 title: …

Card 1 text (one line): …

Card 1 correct zone: …

Card 2 title: …

Card 2 text (one line): …

Card 2 correct zone: …

(repeat for each card)

You can place 2–4 zones and up to 8 cards using this interaction.

When the content is complete: copy and paste the whole brief into the SB and assign a CU ticket.

Technical details for the LT — don't update unless you want the interaction to behave differently.

Layout. The title with the body copy beneath. Below, a dashed tray holding the scenario cards in a two-column grid, each card showing its title, one line of text, and a visible "Assign to zone" select menu. Below the tray, a grid of the labelled drop zones, each with its one-line definition and a dashed drop area. Under the grid, two buttons — "Check my answers" and "Return to tray / Restart" — and a status line. At narrow widths the tray and the zone grid each collapse to one column.

Interaction. The learner drags a card from the tray into any zone's drop area (HTML5 drag events); the target shows a thicker solid border while a drag hovers it. Every card also carries a visible "Assign to zone" select that moves the card to the chosen zone or back to the tray — the mandatory keyboard and touch path. "Check my answers" reveals a feedback line inside each card: a tick or cross icon plus text naming the zone the card belongs in (never colour alone), and the status line announces the score. Moving a card or changing its select clears that card's feedback. "Return to tray / Restart" sends all cards back to the tray and clears all feedback. A polite live region announces each move.

States. Each card is in exactly one container — the tray or one of the zones — all cards in the tray by default. Each card's feedback is hidden, correct (tick), or incorrect/not-placed (cross); all hidden by default. Checking can happen at any time, including with cards still in the tray.

Each placeholder is a single self-contained HTML file using a specific programme branding style. The brief beside it is the complete specification to request the creation of one.

**Purpose.** Let the learner feel how a single parameter changes an outcome by moving a control and watching a chart respond immediately, rather than reading about the relationship.

**Content** — complete each slot with your material. The interaction's built-in labels and prompts stay as they are.

Title: …
Body copy (intro): …

Parameter label (name and range, e.g. "Smoothing window, 1–10"): …
Preset values (two): …
Fixed data series (the values the chart draws): …
Axis caption: …
Consequence text — low values: …
Consequence text — mid values: …
Consequence text — high values: …

When the content is complete: copy and paste the whole brief into the SB and assign a CU ticket.

**Technical details for the LT** — don't update unless you want the interaction to behave differently.

**Layout.** The title with the body copy beneath. Below, a controls panel holding one labelled range slider and two number-chip presets behind a "Presets:" label. Below the controls, an inline SVG chart: the fixed data points drawn as light grey bars, with a blue computed line and dots drawn over them, plus axes, gridlines and axis labels. Below the chart, a live readout line: "Value: N — consequence text…" followed by a text alternative sentence stating the computed line's current range.

**Interaction.** Dragging the slider (or using arrow keys on it — it is a native range input with a visible focus ring) recomputes the line for the chosen value and redraws it; the bars never change. Clicking a preset chip sets the slider to that value; the chip shows a pressed state with a tick icon while the slider matches its value. Every change updates the readout (aria-live polite) and re-reports the document height.

**States.** One per slider value across the parameter's range. The chart is `aria-hidden`; the readout line is the accessible equivalent and changes with every state. No state is terminal; the learner can move freely.

**Interaction name:** `predict-reveal`

**Purpose.** Make the learner commit to a prediction before seeing a result, so the reveal confirms or corrects a genuine guess instead of being passively read.

**Content** — complete each slot with your material. The interaction's built-in labels and prompts stay as they are.

Title: …
Body copy (intro): …

Source material (the tables or figure the learner studies before predicting): …
Prediction question: …
Answer options (one per line, 3–6 chips): …
Correct answer: …
Result (the table or outcome revealed): …
Explanation (one line, shown after the reveal): …

This interaction holds one prediction per instance.

When the content is complete: copy and paste the whole brief into the SB and assign a CU ticket.

---

**Technical details for the LT** — don't update unless you want the interaction to behave differently.

**Layout.** The title with the body copy beneath. Three stacked sections: "1. Source" — the source material; "2. Predict" — the question line, the answer chips and a "Reveal result" button, disabled at rest; "3. Result" — hidden at rest. Below everything, a progress line: one dot and the text "0 of 1 completed".

**Interaction.** Clicking a chip selects it (pressed state with a tick icon) and enables "Reveal result". Clicking reveal shows the result section: the result content, a verdict line with icon — a tick icon and "Correct — your prediction matched the result." on a match, a cross icon and "Not quite — …" naming the correct answer otherwise — the one-line explanation, and a "Restart" button. After reveal the chips lock and the progress line becomes a filled dot with "1 of 1 completed". Restart clears the selection, hides the result, disables reveal, resets progress and moves focus to the first chip. All buttons are native and keyboard operable; every change re-reports the document height.

**States.** Three — unanswered (default: no chip pressed, reveal disabled, result hidden), predicted (one chip pressed, reveal enabled), revealed (result shown with matched or not-matched verdict, chips locked, progress 1 of 1). Exactly one chip can be pressed. The result section exists in the markup and uses the `hidden` attribute; verdict is carried by text plus icon, not colour alone.
